name: Dollar General Corporation

profile.description: Dollar General is the largest U.S. discount retailer by store count, operating 20,000+ small-format stores primarily in rural and suburban communities and selling consumables, household essentials, health and beauty, seasonal and home products at low price points. Founded in 1939 and headquartered in Goodlettsville, Tennessee, it employs about 194,000 people. Q2 FY2026 (ended July 31, 2026) net sales rose 5.2% to $11.3B with same-store sales +3.5% and diluted EPS of $2.48 (+33%), helped partly by tariff refunds worth ~81bps of gross margin. CEO Todd Vasos hands over to JJ Fleeman effective January 1, 2027, and Travis Nixon now leads AI strategy as Chief Data and AI Officer.

innovation.label: DEVELOPING
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Over the past five years DG has extended rather than reinvented its model — continued store growth to 20,000+ locations, fresh produce, DG Media Network and the since-scaled-back pOpshelf concept — while the current 'Back to Basics' program is an operational repair, not a new revenue stream [1][4]. AI Deployment (1/2): DG created an AI role in late 2025 and in June 2026 elevated former Dropbox security AI head Travis Nixon to Chief Data and AI Officer to apply AI across merchandising, supply chain and store operations [2]; no customer-facing AI products or quantified savings have been reported. Market Share (2/2): DG is the category leader in U.S. small-box discount retail by store count and its Q2 FY2026 same-store sales grew 3.5% on 2.0% traffic growth, showing it is gaining trips [1]. Product Pipeline (0/2): No next-generation formats or offerings with named launch dates and revenue visibility were disclosed beyond ongoing store openings and remodels. R&D Intensity (0/1): DG reports no R&D expense; technology investment is below broader retail leaders such as Walmart [3].

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (3/4): DG's mission of 'Serving Others' — affordable essentials close to home for underserved, largely rural communities — is specific and visibly shapes its store-location strategy in places with few retail alternatives [4]. Community Impact (1/2): The Dollar General Literacy Foundation funds adult literacy and education grants in DG communities, but no current-year dollar figure was verified in this review. Employee Retention (0/2): No above-average retention data was found; the 2026 proxy contains a shareholder proposal citing OSHA's 2022 'Severe Violator' designation, a $12M 2024 workplace-safety settlement and further 2025 fines [5]. Insider Buying (0/2): No meaningful net insider buying by executives was identified in the last 12 months.

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on growth-stock metrics (1.74% dividend yield is below the 2% Dividend-sleeve threshold). Forward P/E of 16.33 (1.0) and ROE of 19.69% (1.0, 2x weight) are at target [6]. D/E of 169.8% (including lease liabilities) scores 0.57; TTM revenue growth of 5.2% scores 0.84; the 5yr revenue CAGR of 4.83% (FY2020 $33.75B to FY2025 $42.72B, calculated from reported income statements) scores 0.66 with 2x weight [3][6]. Profit margin of 3.90% scores 0.20, and Yahoo's PEG of 1.65 scores 0.68 with 2x weight [6]. Weighted sum 7.26 / 10 = 7.26, rounded to 7. Liquidity floor easily cleared at ~$316M average daily dollar volume [6].

ai_resilience.label: MODERATE
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (7/9): DG's business is physically stocking and staffing 20,000+ stores that are often the nearest retailer for rural, lower-income households, and coverage of the company frames AI as an efficiency tool, not a disruption threat — Simply Wall St notes the AI hire does not change the main catalyst of store expansion [2]. The residual risk is indirect: AI-optimized delivery and pricing at Walmart and Amazon could narrow DG's convenience advantage over time, which keeps the score below the 8-9 'immune' tier. AI Opportunity (0/1): DG reports no AI-generated revenue; AI is being deployed internally under the new CDAIO [2].

infinite_game.summary: Dollar General's 'Serving Others' purpose is genuine and has shaped where it builds stores for decades, and the Back to Basics reinvestment shows leaders will take an earnings hit to repair the business. But in Sinek's lens the earlier cost-cutting that produced OSHA 'Severe Violator' status reveals a company that let finite targets override its people, and the model has changed little in 87 years. The January 2027 CEO handoff to JJ Fleeman will test whether the reinvestment is a lasting shift or a cyclical correction.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): 'Serving Others' has driven a consistent strategy of placing stores in underserved rural communities and food deserts [4]. It is partially lived — the cost-cutting era that drew OSHA's 'Severe Violator' designation and a $12M safety settlement [5] shows the cause has not consistently overridden financial pressure.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): The 2026 proxy's shareholder proposal cites OSHA's 2022 'Severe Violator' designation for willful and repeat safety violations, a $12M 2024 settlement, additional 2025 fines and a 114:1 CEO-to-median-worker pay ratio [5]. Nine executive changes announced in 2026 and an upcoming CEO transition add instability [2].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): Proxy proponents note DG lags Dollar Tree, Target and Walmart in publishing a comprehensive human rights policy [5], and management commentary centers on its own traffic and price position rather than on learning from rivals' strengths.

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): DG has added fresh food, retail media and new store formats over time [1][4], but the small-box, low-price physical store model is fundamentally the same as decades ago; these are incremental adaptations rather than a reinvention.

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Management accepted a fall in diluted EPS from $10.68 (FY2022) to $5.11 (FY2024) while reinvesting in store labor, inventory and remodels under Back to Basics, and that investment is now showing up in a 33% EPS rebound in Q2 FY2026 [1][3]. It was a costly decision, but a reactive one taken after conditions had already deteriorated.

investment_thesis: Dollar General's turnaround is working. Q2 FY2026 net sales grew 5.2% to $11.3B, same-store sales rose 3.5% with traffic up 2.0%, and diluted EPS jumped 33% to $2.48 [1]. At $135.78 the stock trades at 16.3x forward earnings with 19.7% ROE and roughly $12 per share of TTM free cash flow (P/FCF ~11x) [6], while its rural store base remains the most convenient option for millions of lower-income households. If FY2026 earnings consolidate the recovery from the FY2024 trough of $5.11, there is room for further normalization toward the $10+ EPS the company earned in FY2021-FY2022 [3].
thesis_continued: The bear case is that part of the margin recovery is temporary and the growth runway is short. Tariff refunds contributed about 81bps of Q2 gross margin [1], net margin is only 3.9%, and the 5-year revenue CAGR is 4.83% — a mature, low-growth profile [3][6]. Leverage is meaningful at 169.8% D/E including leases [6], the core customer is financially stretched, and workplace-safety history (OSHA 'Severe Violator', $12M settlement) keeps labor costs and reputational risk elevated [5]. The January 2027 CEO transition to JJ Fleeman lands mid-recovery, and nine leadership changes in 2026 add execution risk [2].
key_catalysts: Q3 FY2026 results (early December 2026) showing whether same-store sales growth of 3.5% and 33% EPS growth hold once tariff-refund benefits fade [1]
AI-driven merchandising, inventory and supply-chain improvements under CDAIO Travis Nixon lifting margins from the current 3.9% net level [2]
Smooth CEO transition to JJ Fleeman on January 1, 2027, preserving Back to Basics momentum [2]
key_risks: Gross-margin normalization as roughly 81bps of tariff-refund benefit in Q2 FY2026 does not recur, pressuring EPS comparisons [1]
Labor and safety liabilities: OSHA 'Severe Violator' history, a $12M 2024 settlement and 2025 fines, plus shareholder pressure for a human rights policy [5]
Leadership turnover: nine executive changes in 2026 and a CEO handoff in January 2027 during an unfinished turnaround [2]
